bib.title: Principles and Algorithms for Forecasting Groups of Time Series: Locality and Globality
bib.venue: preprint (arXiv:2008.00444v3 [cs.LG], 26 Mar 2021; dated March 30, 2021; no journal name printed in the PDF)

read.skipped: Appendix figures (6-24) are plots with no numeric text; only their captions were read.

question: Are global (one function for all series) forecasting methods less general than local ones, and why do they work on heterogeneous sets?
hypothesis: Global methods can match local methods without similar series, and because local complexity grows with the number of series while global stays constant, global models can be more complex and still generalize better.
contributions: Proposition 1: local and global algorithms can produce the same forecasts for time series, with no similarity assumption
Generalization bounds: local complexity grows with set size, global stays constant; implies larger memory for global autoregressions
Extensive empirical study of naive global models (linear, polynomial, deep network, trees, partitioned linear) vs local ets, auto.arima, theta, TBATS, STL-AR
Principles: add features, increase memory, partition (random partitioning as the naive form)

method.summary: Lag-embeds each series at AR order M, stacks all series into one matrix and fits one regression (linear, polynomial deg 2/3, MLP, XGBoost), forecasting recursively one step at a time; compared with local forecast-package methods on MASE across about 17 datasets. Partitioned variant splits the set randomly into 10 equal groups and fits one global linear AR per group.
method.task: univariate forecasting of groups of time series

datasets.name: M4

datasets.split: one-step-ahead out-of-sample error; Fig 6 subsamples M4 to 2000 series per frequency
datasets.preprocessing: each series scaled by MASE scaling as normalisation (Sec 4.3)

other.Table 1 setup: M4 treated as one heterogeneous set, AR(12), one-step-ahead MASE; Cluster = clustered by periodicity (frequency) with one global model per cluster; Glob. Deep+Feat. = fully global deep net with frequency and tsfeatures-type features added as inputs, no partitioning

metrics.name: MASE
metrics.definition: mean absolute scaled error; series scaled as preprocessing so minimising MASE equals minimising MAE on scaled series

eval.protocol: one-step-ahead out-of-sample and in-sample errors; single run per configuration, no seeds or significance tests stated

results.note: Table 1 caption says features give 'equivalent results as clustering'; text says it outperforms all local and the clustered global. Gap to Cluster DeepNet is 0.0036 MASE, single run.

results.setup: M4, one-step-ahead, AR(12), data split by periodicity then one global deep network per cluster

results.claim: Other Table 1 rows: global linear 0.9279, cluster linear 0.8559; local auto.arima 0.7618, ets 0.7644, theta 0.7745.

results.table: Table 1, row Global linear, column MASE

results.claim: Random (not clustered) partitioning is evidence that having similar series is not the cause of good global performance; partitioning reduces sample size yet helps.
results.setup: Sec 5.3: dataset randomly split into 10 equal groups, global linear AR per group; Fig 4 on M4 Monthly, Fig 11 on M1, M3, tourism, M4
results.note: Qualitative: no numeric MASE is printed in the text, only plots. Verbatim sentence: 'Since partitioning is done at random (not clustering), it is strong evidence towards the benefit of raw complexity in a model rather than finding the "right" model, and it shows that having similar series is not the cause of the good performance of global methods.' The sentence is in Sec 5.3 (p14), about the random-partition linear experiment, NOT the M4 Table 1 comparison.

results.claim: The partitioning effect holds in most datasets where the global model is complexity-constrained; authors say it is a showcase of theory, not a recommendation.
results.setup: Fig 11 appendix: global linear vs 10-way random-partitioned linear on M1, M3, tourism, M4
results.note: Verbatim: 'the effect holds (with more or less beneficial impact) in the majority of datasets where the global model is complexity-constrained.' and 'The experiments in this section are meant to showcase the strength of theoretical results because they predict a counter-intuitive effect, they are not a specific recommendation.' Fig 11 caption: 'In the majority of datasets, the Partitioned model outperforms the unpartitioned one, showing that the global linear is constrained by its simplicity (under-fitting).'

results.claim: A global linear AR(25) fitted to 617 M1 Monthly series outperforms state-of-the-art local methods with 25 parameters versus about 1600 for auto.arima.
results.setup: M1 Monthly, global linear AR over all orders (Fig 1)
results.quote:
A single AR(25) — i.e., 25 parameters — can “summarize” the dataset better than models that at
least use 1 parameter per series, e.g. auto.arima needs approximately 1600 parameters to ﬁt the whole set.

results.claim: On M4 Yearly an AR(12) second-degree polynomial global model would have ranked second in the M4 competition.
results.setup: M4 Yearly, global polynomial degree 2, AR(12)
results.quote:
In the M4 yearly an AR(12) polynomial of second degree not only outperforms the local benchmarks, it would have scored second in the M4
competition according to its MASE of 3.01.

results.claim: Scale normalization plus the scale as a feature gives slightly lower relative MASE than normalization alone, both relative to no normalization.
results.setup: deep network AR(12), averaged across datasets, one-step-ahead
results.table: Table 2, row Relative MASE, column Normalization + Scale as Feature
results.note: Relative MAE: normalization 1.0213, with scale feature 0.9959

limits: Bounds are worst-case, agnostic and loose; authors say benefit is insight, not tight guarantees.
Bounds assume independent series and an unknown effective sample size N; dependent groups lose the guarantee.
Better bounds do not imply better out-of-sample error; used as a heuristic.
Clustering analysis is left out of scope; worst-case clustering bounds are vacuous.
No seeds, repeats or significance tests stated; Table 1 differences (0.7596 vs 0.7632) are small and single-run.
Deep network and trees not tuned; authors caution against preferring a model class.
dominick and parts (intermittent) do not show longer memory, better accuracy; authors have no explanation.
Random-partitioning experiments are a demonstration, not a recommendation. Code/data availability not stated in the PDF.
